Release 1 decision: Use 1, 2, 3 and 5 points; split anything larger than 5. Plan an initial 8-10 points per junior developer per two-week sprint.
Rationale: Stories remain small enough to review, test and reassign without hiding multi-sprint work.
Replacement or follow-on: Recalibrate velocity after the first two completed sprints.

Release 1 decision: One human user owns one workspace; the trusted user_id is the ownership key.
Rationale: The pilot does not need organisations, shared workspaces or tenant administration.
Replacement or follow-on: Team and organisational visibility can be added after production identity.

Release 1 decision: Deploy MOSAIC as one Cloud Run instance through the ADA platform path; storage is selected and provisioned separately with Terraform.
Rationale: ADA supplies the framework and Cloud Run deployment path but does not prescribe MOSAIC persistence.
Replacement or follow-on: Multiple instances follow PostgreSQL and shared invocation coordination.

Release 1 decision: mosaic-admin calls a protected pilot endpoint handled by the single MOSAIC process; it never opens mosaic.db directly.
Rationale: This avoids a second SQLite writer and requires no administration UI or container access.
Replacement or follow-on: Remove the endpoint and dedicated administrator secret when governed administration and production identity replace the pilot mechanism.

Release 1 decision: Generate at least 256 random bits, prefix mosaic_r1_, store SHA-256 only and show plaintext once.
Rationale: Opaque high-entropy tokens provide traceable pilot identity without OIDC.
Replacement or follow-on: OIDC replaces human tokens; service identities remain separate.

Release 1 decision: Secure HttpOnly SameSite=Strict cookie with configurable lifetime, default seven days.
Rationale: The browser can remain signed in without exposing the token to JavaScript.
Replacement or follow-on: OIDC session handling replaces it.

Release 1 decision: ADK owns session.db and MOSAIC owns mosaic.db; both reside on Terraform-managed persistent file storage mounted into the single Cloud Run instance.
Rationale: Separate files decouple session cleanup from users and Skill references. Single-process writes bound the risk created by Cloud Run's no-lock NFS mount.
Replacement or follow-on: Recreate both schemas in the single environment PostgreSQL database without migrating pilot data.

Release 1 decision: Store atomic Skill references only. Group assignment expands current members and creates no subscription.
Rationale: Future group changes cannot silently grant a user new Skills.
Replacement or follow-on: Self-service uses the same atomic reference model.

Release 1 decision: Only approved Skills reach main; no commit or tag pinning in the pilot.
Rationale: The controlled catalogue workflow is sufficient at pilot scale.
Replacement or follow-on: Immutable catalogue releases are added if progressive delivery is required.

Release 1 decision: Resolve current workspace Skills only when a new Goal starts and hold the snapshot for that Goal.
Rationale: Administrative changes do not mutate in-flight work.
Replacement or follow-on: Strategic Skill publication retains the same boundary.

Release 1 decision: A standalone JSON file in the private Terraform repository is uploaded as a versioned GCS object and mounted read-only by Cloud Run.
Rationale: It remains reviewed, non-sensitive and environment-specific without complicating image builds.
Replacement or follow-on: A relational Integration publication replaces it.

Release 1 decision: Extend ADA's FastAPI application through a MOSAIC-owned backend bootstrap and deploy that backend to Cloud Run. The Dash frontend is a separate application and executable.
Rationale: MOSAIC retains control of its backend boundary while the frontend can be developed, packaged and deployed independently.
Replacement or follow-on: The frontend may run on Kubernetes or any approved platform and continues to use only the published API.

Release 1 decision: Expose only /api/v1 and required health routes from the MOSAIC Cloud Run backend; reject raw ADA/ADK routes before their handlers. The standalone Dash application reaches MOSAIC through this API.
Rationale: The API is the explicit security and compatibility boundary between independently deployed applications.
Replacement or follow-on: First-class raw-route disabling can be requested from ADA later.

Release 1 decision: Build Dash/Python plus a small local JavaScript SSE client as a separate repository, executable, image and deployment. It is never bundled into the MOSAIC process or image.
Rationale: The frontend can run on Kubernetes or another suitable platform and change independently while MOSAIC remains an API-only backend.
Replacement or follow-on: A React replacement remains optional because the API boundary is technology-neutral.

Release 1 decision: Run one Cloud Run instance, allow one active invocation per conversation and serialise MOSAIC administrative writes in process; return exact HTTP 409 and do not queue.
Rationale: This prevents conflicting ADK session updates with minimal machinery.
Replacement or follow-on: Shared production limits and 429 responses are deferred.

Release 1 decision: Browser or SSE disconnect does not cancel; explicit Cancel is terminal; Cloud Run instance termination kills in-flight work.
Rationale: Users can close the browser and later see the persisted completed response.
Replacement or follow-on: Cross-replica coordination is added with production scaling.

Release 1 decision: Persist ADK sessions indefinitely in mounted session.db; provide no deletion UI or automated retention.
Rationale: The pilot can retain history; cleanup can stop MOSAIC and remove session.db without deleting mosaic.db.
Replacement or follow-on: Configurable inactive-session retention follows production usage.

Release 1 decision: Mounted storage protects completed sessions and MOSAIC metadata from Cloud Run instance replacement; in-flight work is not resumed.
Rationale: Pilot persistence is required, but production high availability, backup and recovery targets are not.
Replacement or follow-on: PostgreSQL backup, restore and multi-instance coordination follow agreed service targets.

Release 1 decision: All endpoints are development-only and MCP servers run explicitly read-only.
Rationale: This permits deferral of the security shim and delegated RBAC.
Replacement or follow-on: MCP shim and provider-specific RBAC precede sensitive data access.

Release 1 decision: Use existing ADA/GCP telemetry for the pilot and add only correlation metadata.
Rationale: Duplicate audit and chargeback stores are premature.
Replacement or follow-on: Add a usage ledger only if production telemetry lacks user-level attribution.
